Private Grand Canyon Tour from Scottsdale and Phoenix

A private Grand Canyon tour from Scottsdale is one vehicle and one chauffeur, booked by the hour for a 14-hour day to the South Rim and back: your group, your stops, nobody else's schedule. The 14-seat Executive Black Sprinter is $145 an hour and that day bills 12 hours: $1,740 before 8% tax, roughly $124 a seat with 14 aboard. The published drive: "About 3 hours 30 minutes each way from Scottsdale." Below: the honest comparison with a shared seat and with driving yourself, where the hours go, which vehicle fits, and how the quote is built. Reservations: (623) 986-6339.

Last updated: September 17, 2026

What is a private Grand Canyon tour from Scottsdale?

One vehicle and one chauffeur, booked by the hour for a 14-hour day to the South Rim and back — not a seat on somebody else's coach. In the 14-seat Executive Black Sprinter at $145 an hour that day bills 12 hours: $1,740 before 8% tax. You buy the whole vehicle for a window of time: your group decides who is aboard, where it stops and how long it stays, in writing before anyone pays. It suits the parties a shared seat serves badly — a family pacing the day around grandparents or small children, a company taking clients out of a conference, anyone who would rather not drive. Per head the arithmetic is plainer than it looks: the Executive Black Sprinter splits $1,740 across 14 seats, about $124 each; the 56-Passenger Motorcoach splits $3,900 across 56. Those are the current published hourly rates across this day.

Is a private tour better than a shared bus tour or driving yourself?

Better is the wrong test; different is the right one. The 3 shapes differ in what you buy, who sets the stops and who drives home in the dark. This page sells the vehicle for 14 hours, never a seat, and quotes no price but its own. A seat on a shared coach is a fixed product: a published departure point, a published route, a fixed dwell time at each stop. For one or two travellers it is usually cheaper, and stops being the obvious choice once seats add up. Driving yourself buys control at the price of the drive: 7 hours at the wheel, most of the return in the dark, one person watching the road instead of the canyon. The private day sits between them, and will not beat a single shared seat on price — no third-party fare appears here, because we cannot source one. How does a Grand Canyon day from Scottsdale run, hour by hour?

Start early and the arithmetic works: a 6:00 AM pickup, 3 hours 30 minutes north, 7 hours on the rim and the same drive back puts the group home at 8:00 PM. That is the whole 14-hour window this day is priced at. The block the desk works from says it plainly: "One pickup address for the whole party and one phone we call, and expect an early start. The day is booked as a single hourly charter, so the vehicle and chauffeur stay with you from the first pickup to the last drop-off — the clock does not stop at the rim." An hourly charter buys time, not mileage, so an extra overlook costs nothing — but one nobody wrote down was never in the route. The table is the published day laid over the published drive, not a promise about traffic. For longer than it allows: "Groups either book a single long day or add a night in Tusayan or Flagstaff." What is worth seeing on the South Rim in one day?

The South Rim is the rim this page books, and the 3 anchors its destination page names fill a day: Mather Point for the first view, Grand Canyon Village and its lodges, and Desert View to the east, joined on foot by the paved Rim Trail between the overlooks. Quoted as this site already publishes it: "Grand Canyon Village centers around the historic buildings and lodges along the South Rim. The Village includes the iconic El Tovar Hotel, Bright Angel Lodge, and numerous viewpoints. Mather Point offers the classic first view, while the Rim Trail connects overlooks for miles. Bright Angel Trail and South Kaibab Trail provide canyon access. Desert View to the east features Mary Colter's Watchtower. The park operates free shuttle buses connecting major points during busy seasons." What this page will not do is turn that into ranger talks, shuttle times or opening hours: those change, and they are the park's to publish. The chauffeur handles the driving and the waiting — and the thing guests forget they may ask: "Ask your chauffeur for anything. Stops, temperature, volume, a photo. Really."

Which vehicle fits the group on a Grand Canyon day?

Group size decides it, and 8 vehicles are offered for a day tour — proper forward-facing seats, never a limo or a party layout. They run from 14 seats at $1,740 to 56 at $3,900 for the same 14-hour day. Every row prices the same day: the published hourly rate times 12 billable hours, which is what 14 requested hours come to once the ladder takes 2 off. The per-seat column divides that by seated capacity: friends splitting one fare, never a fare sold per person. The Executive Black Sprinter and Executive White Sprinter share a rate; past 14 travellers it is the Mini Bus (24 Pax), Executive Mini Bus — Grech (27 Pax) and Executive Mini Coach (29 Pax). Cabin space is the second question: "Pack for a long day out rather than a move: layers for the rim, water, and room for what you buy. If anyone is being dropped at an airport afterwards with full luggage, say so when you book so the fit is confirmed in writing." What does a private Grand Canyon day tour cost?

A 14-hour day in the 14-seat Executive Black Sprinter is $1,740 before 8% tax — $145 an hour across 12 billable hours, because 14 requested hours earn 2 free ones. Split 14 ways that is roughly $124 a seat for the day. Three rules build every number here, none specific to the canyon: the day is priced by the hour against the vehicle's published minimum, hours above the ladder's rungs earn free hours, and 8% tax is the only addition. The drive is not a separate line — "the drive each way is inside the booked window, not on top of it". The Executive Black Sprinter is the least expensive day at $1,740, the 56-Passenger Motorcoach the least expensive seat at $70 with its 56 seats used. Pay 50% today by card; the balance is charged 48 hours before pickup. Availability is date-specific, so request a current quote for yours.

What is included on the day, and what is not?

Included is the vehicle, the chauffeur and every mile of the 14-hour window, plus bottled water — the only complimentary amenity. Not included is what the park and the Village charge for, and the page says which is which before you book rather than at the gate. In its own words: "Bottled water is on board and it is the only complimentary amenity; park entry, meals and anything bought on the way are yours." Park entry is the item groups most often assume is bundled, and it is not: "Park entry, permits and site access are set by the operators there." One house rule matters more here than on a night out: "No eating or food inside the vehicle. Drinks are fine; snacks wait for the next stop." What the online quote cannot price goes to a person: "Anything the online quote cannot price — an unusual route, a multi-vehicle movement, a vehicle we hold for request only — goes to the reservations desk and comes back as a written quote before any card is charged." Reservations: (623) 986-6339.

Can the trip add Sedona, or start outside Scottsdale?

Both, and each has its own booking. Sedona and the canyon together are a separate published tour rather than a longer version of this one, and a pickup can start in any of the 10 metro cities with a service-area page. Asking one 14-hour day to cover both properly is the commonest way a good itinerary is spoiled: the detour comes out of rim time. Red rocks and the rim together is the combined tour; Sedona alone is the red-rocks tour. The published service areas are Scottsdale, Phoenix, Paradise Valley, Tempe, Mesa, Chandler, Gilbert, Glendale, Cave Creek and San Tan Valley, and pickup is a street address rather than a zone.

How it works on the day

Good to know. Bottled water is on board and it is the only complimentary amenity; park entry, meals and anything bought on the way are yours.

  • Where we meet you: One pickup address for the whole party and one phone we call, and expect an early start. The day is booked as a single hourly charter, so the vehicle and chauffeur stay with you from the first pickup to the last drop-off — the clock does not stop at the rim.
  • Luggage: Pack for a long day out rather than a move: layers for the rim, water, and room for what you buy. If anyone is being dropped at an airport afterwards with full luggage, say so when you book so the fit is confirmed in writing. The Executive Black Sprinter is rated for up to 40 bags.
  • What we can and cannot do: The day is priced by the hour with a four-hour minimum, and the drive each way is inside the booked window, not on top of it. Park entry, permits and site access are set by the operators there; where a destination needs a commercial access review we confirm it in writing before accepting a booking. Anything the online quote cannot price — an unusual route, a multi-vehicle movement, a vehicle we hold for request only — goes to the reservations desk and comes back as a written quote before any card is charged.
  • What it costs: 14 hours in the Executive Black Sprinter (seats 14): the hour ladder gives you 2 free hours, so you pay for 12: 12 × $145 = $1,740. Add 8% Arizona tax; there is no booking fee and no fuel fee. How the rest settles depends on how you pay: a 50% deposit holds the date and the balance is charged to the card on file 48 hours before pickup; paying in full at checkout leaves nothing else due before your ride; a payment link from the reservations desk is due before the ride.
